newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end broadly lower after seesaw session.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end broadly lower after seesaw session.

text.p: Stocks ended sharply lower Friday after being whipsawed by a series of computerized programme trades that sent blue-chips to their third straight loss.
As fears of rising interest rates mounted, the Dow Jones industrial average fell 59.27 points to end the week at 6,696.48, down nearly 200 points from its record close of 6,883.90 on Tuesday.
The index was off 136.62 since last Friday, making it the first full week this year in which it lost ground.
In the broader market, declining issues outpaced gainers by 1,699 to 837 on heavy volume of 546 million on the New York Stock Exchange.
Broader indicators mirrored the Dow's decline and a number of analysts said the retreat by stocks was looking more and more like the start of a corrective phase for the market.

Investors also grew more concerned about interest rates, which edged still higher as the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond fell 11/32, pushing the yield up to 6.89 percent from 6.86 percent at Thursday's close. The bond's price and yield move in opposite directions.

"The bond market is about 5 percent off its high, and for the stock market to decline about 5 percent off its high would not be out of the realm of the possible," said Peter Green, vice president of technical research at Gruntal & Co.
In contrast with Thursday, when stocks met with a sudden and sharp wave of programme selling at the end of the day, Friday's session was marked by sweeping advances and declines of up to 90 points.
Several times during the course of the day, buy programmes lifted the Dow up from its lows, as fund managers put to work the vast amounts of retirement account cash still at their disposal.
"People still bought the dip," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "The deployment of funds continues."
Even as the fund money was providing something of a safety net for stocks, some analysts were mulling the prudence of buying at these near-record levels, even on dips.
"This is very different because for the first time in the last five years, the market has become overvalued," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.
Johnson said based on an analysis of corporate earnings and price-to-earnings ratios, the market had reached a level where substantial further gains would be hard to come by.
Hardest hit were financial and transportation stocks, which are particularly sensitive to fluctuations in interest rates.
Among major banks, Citicorp slid 3-3/8 to 109-3/8, BankAmerica Corp. fell 3-1/8 to 105-1/8 and Chase Manhattan Corp. shed 2 to 89-1/8.
American Airlines parent AMR Corp. fell 1-1/8 to 84-1/2, and Delta Air Lines Inc. dipped 1-1/4 to 81-1/8.
Many technology stocks also suffered losses, pulling the Nasdaq Composite index down 14.54 points to 1,363.83. The index was up 14.78 on the week.
Leading the decline was Cascade Communications Corp., which plummeted 23-1/8 or 36 percent to 41 after reporting fourth quarter earnings late Thursday.
Cascade's earnings rose sharply in the quarter, and in fact the company met analysts' estimates.
But Wall Street analysts focused instead on matters that foreshadowed slower growth, like Cascade's slower collections of accounts receivable.
The concern spilled over to some other networking equipment shares. Cisco Systems Inc. fell 3-1/8 to 68-5/8 and NYSE-listed shares in Canada-based Newbridge Networks Corp. fell 1-1/2 to 32-5/8.

The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 7.04 to 770.52, leaving that index 5.65 points lower for the week. The American Stock Exchange index edged down 1.53 to 588.16, down 1.79 on the week.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks slid 3.64 to 405.51. The average price per share fell 38 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,467.206, down 68.293, or 0.91 percent. The index was down 34.625 on the week.
